FOREWORD This Indian Standard ( Second Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards on 30 September 1988, after the draft finalized by the Silk, Man-Made Fibre and Products Sectional Committee had been approved by the Textile Division Council. Lining fabrics are used for various apparels, such as blouses, frocks, coats, etc. It is important that the lining fabric should withstand the treatments to which the apparels are exposed during actual use. Moreover, its durability should be comparable to that of the original apparel for which it is used. In India, lining fabrics used are made mainly from rayon or cotton or continuous filament viscose rayon yarn as warp and cotton or a blend of cotton with staple viscose yarn as weft. However, from the consumer point of view, the ultimate performance requirements of lining fabrics are more important than the constructional particulars which go on changing with time. This standard specifies the requirements for general characteristics like appearance, feel and shade ( 5.1 ); flammability and soil release efficiency of fabric ( Table 1, Sl No. 6 and 7 ) which are made optional as per the agreement between the buyer and the seller. Lining cloth had been covered by three separate standards, namely, IS 2136 : 1974 `Specification for rayon satin lining cloth (Jirst revision )`, IS 2228 : 1964 `Specification for rayon mix lining cloth ( revised )`, and IS 7392 : 1974 `Specification for rayon taffeta lining cloth', which specified the constructional particulars that have changed with the passage of time. The present revision is a unification of these three standards under the designation IS 2136 : 1988. Subsequently This standard specifies toleIS 2228 : 1964 and IS 7392 : 1974 stand superseded by this revision. rances in respect of linear density of warp and weft :yarns, endsldm, mass/m3, picks/dm, fibre content, length and width of fabric keeping in view Its end-use and optimum quality. WOVEN FLAT LINING FABRICS FOR APPARELS - SPECIFICATION ( Second Revision )
1 SCOPE 1.1This standard specifies the requirements for woven flat lining fabrics composed of man-made fibres or their blends with other fibres used for apparels.
1.2 This specification is not applicable to woven pile, woven fusible, firebonded fusible, sliverknit pile and sheepskin lining fabrics. 2 REFERENCES 2.1 The Indian Standards listed in Annex A are necessary adjuncts to this standard. 3 MANUFACTURE 3.1 Yarn In case of lining fabrics made of man-made fibres or their blends, continuous filament yarn Table 1 Reqoirements

The lining fabric shall be uniformly woven with firm selvedges and should be free from weaving and processing defects ( see also Annex B ). The constructional particulars of some important lining fabrics are given in Annex C for guidance only. ANNEX B ( Clauses 3.2 and 9.1 )
CATEGORIZATION OF FLAWS B-l SERIOUS FLAWS B-l.1 The serious flaws include: a) One or more ends missing in the body of the material throughout its length, or more than three ends missing at a place 3 and running over 600 mm or prominently noticeable double end running througbout the length of the piece; Undressed snarls noticeable over a length b) exceeding 5 percent of the length of the piece;

I6 2136: 1988 c) Bad smashes definitely rupturing the texture of the fabric; d) Holes, cut or tear; e) Reed marks prominently noticeable over a length exceeding 5 percent of the length of the piece; f) Defective or damaged selvedge noticeable over a length exceeding 5 percent of the length of the piece; g) Very large floats; h) Missing weft across full width for more than 6 mm; and j) Mechanical damage, abrasion marks affecting the strength of the fabric. 8-2 MAJOR FLAWS 32.1 The major flaws include a) Weft crack or two or more missing picks less than 6 mm across the width of the fabric; b) Weft bar due to the difference in raw material, count, twist, lustre, colour, shade or pick spacing of adjacent groups of weft yarns; ends running c) More than two adjacent parallel or broken or missing end extending beyond 100 mm; d) Noticeable warp or weft floats over 6'5 mm square or if over 13 mm long or broad, floating over more than four threads; e) Noticeable oil or other stains in the fabric unless the causes are known and the effects are known to be harmless; f) Prominently noticeable slub; d Conspicuous broken pattern; h) Gout due to foreign matter, usually lint or waste, woven into the fabrics; 3 Hard inclusions; k) Badly made pull backs; 4 Prominent selvedge defects, that is, weak, slack, wavy, tight or scalloped selvedge; d Significant shading or listing in fabrics having a gradual change in tone or depth of shade of fabric ( excluding selvedge or border running parallel to the selvedge ); P) Coloured flecks; 9) Blurred or dark patch; r) Patchy, streaky or uneven dyeing; s) Dye bar; t) Printing defect which mars the general appearance of the fabric; and bars of relatively tight or u) Longitudinal slack warp threads.

Standard

Mark

The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Br~eau Q/" Ztuliurl Stmtlurtls Act, lY86 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by RIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards.

Bureau of Indian Standards

BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote harmonius development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to connected matters in the country.
